true but not true. all human DNA is basically the same, but depending on the cell it came from it can have varying amounts of the entire genome. Red blood cells for example have fragments of the human genome, while white blood cells have most if not the entire DNA cache. Skin cells have the entire DNA cache but much of it is inactive as skin cells at the surface of the body tend to be end stage cells destined for keritinization. Hair itself is mostly keratin but the root cells contain the whole genome as well.

Now if you get into epigenitics you can tell what genes are being primarily expressed at a given time. Using what we have available from medical science we should be able to distinguish at a limited basis between tissues and organs. So you might be able to tell if a limb is in a hotdog or an eye. Or even skin. The sample size becomes the problem though.

EDIT: gametes are haploid and can be easily distinguished from other cells based on that as well as the fact that many epigenetic markers are missing from gamete DNA. This is because developmentally humans start very close to blank slate. Not exactly but close.
